readerTitle: A pivot isn't starting over. It's choosing what to keep.
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (보냉 상자 제조사, 요가 스튜디오 예약 앱) + 가상 적용 (베이커리) · 피벗 유형은 Eric Ries의 분류를 참고
insight: 피벗은 무엇을 바꾸느냐보다 무엇을 지키느냐로 고른다. 지킬 것을 먼저 정하면 선택지가 좁혀진다.
misconception: 피벗은 사업을 통째로 갈아엎고 새로 시작하는 것이다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. 8장 'Pivot (or Persevere)'의 피벗 유형 목록
보냉 상자 제조사, 예약 앱, 베이커리는 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: The Lean Startup 8장의 피벗 유형 목록(zoom-in, zoom-out, customer segment, customer need, platform, business architecture, value capture, engine of growth, channel, technology)을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 '약 10가지(about ten)'로만 적었습니다.
2번 카드의 '주문 40% 감소'는 가상 수치입니다. 혈액 샘플 운송의 온도 요건은 일반적인 설명으로만 썼으며 구체적 규정은 다루지 않았습니다.
6번 카드 목록은 Ries 목록 중 업종을 가리지 않는 7개만 골라 쉬운 말로 바꿨습니다. 원문 용어와 뜻이 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two companies pivoted in the same month.
body: One kept its product and found a new customer. The other kept its customers and threw away almost all of its product.
Both called it a pivot. They were very different moves, and the difference starts with one question: *what are you keeping?*

image.label: Two doors: one with a crate, one with a phone screen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 갈림길에 선 두 사람. 한 명은 보냉 상자를 그대로 들고 새 방향으로, 다른 한 명은 휴대폰 화면에서 버튼 하나만 떼어 들고 걸어감. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Your biggest customers are leaving.
body: You make reusable insulated crates for meal-kit companies. Your two biggest clients just cut orders by 40%.
Meanwhile, three medical couriers have asked whether your crates could carry lab samples that must stay cold for hours. What do you do?

options.text: Cut prices to win back the meal-kit clients
options.feedback: It buys time and keeps the relationships. But you keep everything, including the shrinking market that caused the problem.

options.text: Test the same crate with the medical couriers
options.feedback: You keep your factory, your design and your know-how about cold. Only the customer changes, so a test is cheap and fast.

options.text: Use the factory to make something new, like garden planters
options.feedback: You keep the machines but drop your best asset: knowing how to keep things cold. That's closer to a new company than a pivot.

cards.title: The crate maker changed one thing.
body: Selling to couriers meant new paperwork and a slower sales process. But most of the business carried over intact.

breakdown.label: Product
breakdown.detail: Same crate, plus a temperature log

cards.title: The booking app kept one button.
body: A software startup sold a booking app to yoga studios. Studios signed up, but few paid, and most ignored the calendar and payment tools.
The usage data showed one feature used every day: automatic texts that offer a cancelled spot to the next person on the waitlist.
The team cut everything else and sold **the waitlist tool alone** to the same studios. Same customers, a much smaller product.

image.label: An app screen shrinking down to one feature
image.brief: 예약 앱 화면에서 달력, 결제 등 여러 기능 블록이 흐려지며 떨어져 나가고, '대기자 알림' 블록 하나만 밝게 남아 확대되는 장면. 실제 앱 UI나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Types of pivots
body: A **pivot** is a change to one part of your business that keeps what you have learned. It is a turn, not a restart.
Pivots are named by **what changes**. The crate maker made a *customer segment* pivot: same product, new customer. The app made a *zoom-in* pivot: one feature became the whole product.
Eric Ries listed about ten types in *The Lean Startup* (2011). The names matter less than the habit of asking which part is moving.

cards.title: The common types, by what changes
body: Each type changes one part and keeps the rest.
list: **Zoom-out:** the product becomes one part of something bigger
**Customer need:** same customer, a different problem to solve
**Channel:** same product, a new way to reach buyers
**Value capture:** same product, a new way to charge, like renting instead of selling
**Technology:** same solution, built a different way
cards.callout: Decide what you'll keep first. That narrows the options fast.

cards.title: Change one thing, not five.
body: Change several parts at once and you are really starting over. If it works, you won't know why.
What you keep can also be the problem. If nobody wants the crate, a new customer won't save it. And pivots have costs: some customers, staff and investors signed up for the old plan.
Treat the new direction as a test with a clear signal, not a final answer.

cards.title: Now it's a bakery.
body: Your bakery's walk-in sales are falling. But local offices keep emailing to order birthday cakes for staff, often several a month, and they rarely ask about price.
Which move fits what you've learned?

options.text: Offer offices a monthly staff-birthday cake plan
options.feedback: You keep your recipes, kitchen and skills, and change the customer and how you charge. It follows demand you can already see.

options.text: Open a second shop on a busier street
options.feedback: More foot traffic might help, but it's a costly bet on the customers who are fading. It ignores the signal from the offices.

options.text: Become a full corporate caterer with lunches and staff
options.feedback: It chases the same customer, but changes the product, kitchen and team at once. If it struggles, you won't know which change caused it.

cards.title: Pick what to keep, then change one thing.
body: A good pivot carries your strongest asset into a new direction. Name that asset before you name the new plan.
**Try it today:** write your business as five parts: customer, problem, product, channel, how you charge. Circle the one you'd never give up. Star the one you'd change first.
